question: to the Commission Alex Agius Saliba (S&D), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Jana Toom (Renew), Maria Walsh (PPE) Subject:

In June 2023, the Commission presented the comprehensive approach to mental health, aimed at placing mental health on an equal footing with physical health. However, while the initiative includes actions on prevention, access to care and societal resilience, it lacks a longterm policy framework and new actions beyond 2026. With the current programming period ending, concerns arise about the absence of a clear EUlevel vision for mental health after 2026, despite strong political commitments from President von der Leyen and Parliament’s calls for sustained EU leadership in this area. 1.
How does the Commission intend to ensure political and policy continuity on mental health at EU level after the conclusion of the flagship actions of the comprehensive approach in 2026?
Does the Commission plan to propose a European mental health strategy or equivalent framework to succeed the comprehensive approach, and if so, within what timeframe?

How will lessons learned from the implementation of the comprehensive approach be collected and used to inform future EU-level mental health policy, including its integration into broader frameworks such as the European Semester, the European Pillar of Social Rights, and the future multiannual financial framework?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) Promoting good mental health, in particular of children and young people, is a priority for the Commission. Its Communication on a comprehensive approach to mental health1 from 2023 has been instrumental in this respect. The Communication has 20 flagship initiatives and almost EUR 1.3 billion in funding opportunities. The Commission currently focuses on the implementation of the Communication and related actions under the EU4Health programme, such as the joint actions MENTOR2 and PRISM3. To promote the mental health of young people online, the Commission adopted in February 2026 an action plan against cyberbullying4. Moving forward, the Commission will focus on the impact of the use of social media and screens on youth mental and physical health. In her Political Guidelines5, the President of the Commission committed to launch an EU-wide inquiry on the topic which is in preparation. It will take into account the work and outcomes of the panel of experts to address online safety for children announced by the Commission’s President in her State of the Union 2025 speech6 and kicked off in March 20267. The Commission’s proposal for the next multiannual financial framework provides funding opportunities for mental health, e.g. in line with the specific activities listed in Article 37(1) of the proposed European Competitiveness Fund. The Commission’s proposal on national and regional partnership plans (NRPPs) envisions that Member States could use their NRPPs to address health system challenges identified in the European Semester and in line with the objectives in Article 3(1), point (c)(iv) of the proposal for NRRPs.
